113.sense: Jews say Christians stand on nothing and Christians say Jews stand on nothing, though both groups read a Book. Unlettered people who know nothing are said to say something similar, and the verse leaves the dispute to Allah, who will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection over what they differed about.

notes.t: Allah judging between differing groups on the Day of Resurrection, phrased almost identically, closes a list of religious communities in Surah Al-Hajj.

links.why: the same judgment on the Day of Resurrection, closing a longer list of groups that differed

114.sense: The question, who is more unjust than one who bars Allah's name from being mentioned in His mosques and works toward their ruin, has an implied answer: no one. Such people, the verse says, have no right to enter those mosques except in fear, and disgrace in this world is paired with a greater punishment still ahead in the next.

notes.t: Barring the Prophet and the believers from the Sacred Mosque is named directly, using a related root for obstruction, in Surah Al-Fath.

links.why: the same act of barring people from a mosque of Allah, named directly at Al-Masjid al-Haram

115.sense: East and west both belong to Allah, so wherever a person turns, Allah's face is met there. The verse states a scope, not a rule for the direction of prayer; the surah later fixes the qibla for the standing prayer, while this verse addresses something wider than any one direction.

notes.t: The Prophet is reported to have prayed voluntary prayers on his mount facing whatever direction it was travelling, citing this verse for it.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn 'Umar

notes.t: The surah later fixes a specific direction for the obligatory prayer, turning the face toward the Sacred Mosque, which this wider verse does not set aside.

links.why: the qibla later fixed for prayer in this same surah, read alongside this verse's wider claim

116.sense: The claim that Allah has taken a son is answered with glory be to Him and then with ownership: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and all of it is obedient to Him. A son implies a peer or an heir; the verse answers with total ownership instead, leaving no room for either.

notes.t: The same claim and a dramatic answer, that the heavens are almost torn apart by it, are given at length in Surah Maryam.

links.why: the same claim answered at greater length, with the heavens described as almost splitting apart at it

117.sense: Badi', Originator, names Allah as the one who brought the heavens and the earth into being without a prior model. What follows is the mechanism: when He decrees a matter, He only says to it be, and it is, no material and no interval between the word and the thing.

notes.t: The same short command, be, and it is, recurs for the creation of Isa without a father, among other places.

links.why: the same command used for a specific creation, Isa formed without a father

118.sense: People with no knowledge ask why Allah does not speak to them directly or send them a sign of their own. The verse notes that people before them said the same thing in the same words, and calls their hearts alike, naming the demand a pattern of ordinary human sameness rather than a distinct achievement, set against believers for whom the signs are already clear.

notes.t: The same demand, to see angels sent down or to see Allah directly, is described from people who reject any meeting with their Lord, in Surah Al-Furqan.

links.why: the same kind of demand, to see angels or to see Allah directly, from a different group

words.g: as a bringer of glad tidings

119.sense: The Prophet is told plainly what he was sent for, a bringer of good news and a warner, sent with truth, and told he will not be questioned about the people of the Blaze. Responsibility for those who end up there is not laid on the one who delivered the warning.

notes.t: The same pairing, bringer of good news and warner, describes the Prophet's mission again in Surah Al-Ahzab.

links.why: the same description of the mission, bringer of good news and warner, repeated later in the Qur'an

120.sense: Neither the Jews nor the Christians will be pleased until the Prophet follows their religion, so the instruction given him is to say that Allah's guidance is the guidance, not a guidance among others. Following their desires after knowledge has already come is named as leaving him without protector or helper from Allah, the same closing pair used earlier in the passage.

notes.t: The same closing pair, no protector and no helper besides Allah, was already used in this passage a few verses earlier.
Millah, translated religion here, is the same word the surah later uses for the millah of Ibrahim, the standard the coming verses measure true religion against.

links.why: the identical closing phrase, no protector and no helper, used earlier in this same passage
the millah of Ibrahim named soon after, the standard the surah sets against this warning

121.sense: Those given the Book who recite it as it should be recited are the ones who truly believe in it, recitation done rightly folded into belief rather than separated from it. Whoever disbelieves in it, on the other side, is named among the losers, closing the passage on a division drawn by response to the Book itself.

notes.t: The same distinction is drawn in Al 'Imran: not all the People of the Book are the same, some of them stand in prayer through the night reciting the verses of Allah.

links.why: the exception named directly, a standing group among the People of the Book who recite rightly and believe

122.sense: The address returns to Bani Israil, repeating almost word for word an appeal made earlier in the surah. They are told to remember two things together: the favor given them and their having been preferred above the peoples of their age. The next verse turns that memory toward a warning about a day when no one can help another.

notes.t: The same call, favor and preference over the worlds in the same formula, opens an earlier passage addressed to Bani Israil.
Elsewhere the preference is spelled out as the Book, judgment and prophethood given to Bani Israil, which fixes it as a historical grant rather than a permanent rank over later communities.

links.why: the same appeal to Bani Israil, worded almost identically
the favor spelled out in full: the Book, judgment and prophethood, with the same closing phrase, preferred over the worlds

123.sense: The warning names a day and revokes four kinds of help in a row: no soul can settle another's account, no ransom is taken in place of the reckoning, no intercession helps, and no rescue arrives from outside. Each clause closes off one thing a person might otherwise be counting on.

notes.t: An earlier verse in the surah opens with the same warning to Bani Israil, in the same four clauses, with ransom and intercession given in reverse order.
ʿadl here is a substitute paid to cancel a claim, a ransom, not the later sense of the word as justice.

links.why: the same warning stated earlier in the surah, with the middle two clauses in reverse order

124.sense: Ibrahim's Lord tests him with a set of commands, called only "words," and he carries every one of them out. On that record he is named a leader for people. He asks that the leadership reach his descendants as well, and the answer draws a line: the covenant does not reach whoever does wrong.

notes.t: kalimāt, "words," is left unspecified; exegetes read it as the run of tasks and trials across Ibrahim's life rather than one single test.
The command to sacrifice his son, given in a vision, is called there "a clear trial": likely one of the words Ibrahim was tested with and fulfilled.
imām names a model that is followed, not a ruler; the word later also names one who leads people in prayer.

links.why: the sacrifice trial itself, told in full, likely one of the words tested here
Allah's choosing of Ibrahim's family over the worlds, the wider claim behind naming him a leader for people

words.g: and those who seclude themselves there

125.sense: The House is set as a place people return to again and again and a place of security, and the hearers are told to take the station of Ibrahim, the stone he stood on, as a place of prayer. Ibrahim and Isma'il are then charged to keep the House pure for four groups gathered there: those circling it, those secluded in devotion, and those bowing and prostrating in prayer.

notes.t: mathābatan carries the sense of a place returned to again and again, from the root th-w-b, related to thawāb, a return given for what is spent.
The same charge to purify the House for those who circle it, stand, bow and prostrate is repeated in the account of Ibrahim being shown its site.
The House is called the first one established for people anywhere, holding clear signs including the station of Ibrahim.

links.why: the same instruction to purify the House, in the fuller account of it being shown to Ibrahim
the House named the first one built for people, with the station of Ibrahim inside it

126.sense: Ibrahim prays for the land to be made secure and its people given fruit, narrowing the request to those among them who believe in Allah and the last day. The answer widens the scope back out: the disbeliever too is given a brief enjoyment, before being driven to the Fire's punishment, a poor destination.

notes.t: Ibrahim's own prayer names only the believers; the answer corrects the scope, extending provision to everyone for a time regardless of belief.
A fuller version of this prayer, made after Ibrahim settles his offspring by the House, asks that it be secure and that people's hearts be drawn toward it.
The same pattern is applied to disbelievers generally: their movement through the land is a brief enjoyment, and then Hell is their resting place.

links.why: Ibrahim's fuller prayer for the land, asking that hearts be inclined toward his offspring there
the same pattern stated of disbelievers generally, brief enjoyment then the Fire

127.sense: Ibrahim raises the foundations of the House together with Isma'il, and the verse moves directly into their prayer over it: accept this from us, You are the Hearing, the Knowing. The building and the plea for it to be accepted are given in a single breath.

notes.t: The verb yarfaʿu is in the present tense though the event is past, putting the reader inside the act of building rather than reporting it as already finished.
Ibrahim and the site of the House appear again together in the passage where he is shown its place and charged to purify it.

links.why: Ibrahim shown the site of the House and charged over it, the companion passage to this scene

128.sense: The prayer continues, asking that Ibrahim and Isma'il themselves be submitting to Allah and that a nation from their own descendants be submitting as well. They ask to be shown their rites and to have their repentance accepted, naming Allah as the one who turns to His servants and is merciful.

notes.t: manāsik, rites, is the same word later used for the rites of Hajj; here it names something Ibrahim and Isma'il must be shown, not something they devised.
A later verse calls this community by the religion of their father Ibrahim, who named them submitting ones (Muslims) beforehand.

links.why: the community named after Ibrahim's own naming, tying this prayer to a later description of the same submission

129.sense: The prayer closes with a request for a messenger from among their own descendants, one who recites Allah's signs to them, teaches them the Book and wisdom, and purifies them. The four things asked for here reappear almost verbatim as a description of the Prophet's own mission.

notes.t: Allah describes sending an unlettered messenger from among the Arabs' own number who recites His verses to them, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom: the same four verbs, in nearly the same order.
A report has the Prophet ﷺ say that he is "the supplication of my father Ibrahim." It is carried in Ahmad's Musnad and its chain is discussed among the hadith scholars.
notes.src: Ahmad, Musnad, from al-ʿIrbād ibn Sāriyah; chain discussed

links.why: the same four things asked for here, recite, teach the Book, teach wisdom, purify,describing the Prophet's mission

130.sense: The question is rhetorical: who would turn away from Ibrahim's way except someone who deceives himself. Allah's own regard for Ibrahim follows as the answer to that question: chosen in this world, and counted among the righteous in the next.

notes.t: safiha nafsahu, literally "made his own self foolish," puts the harm of turning away on the one who turns, not on Ibrahim or his standing.
Ibrahim is called a nation obedient to Allah, given good in this world and placed among the righteous in the next, in nearly the same closing formula.

links.why: the same pairing, good given in this world, a place among the righteous in the next,stated of Ibrahim directly

131.sense: The command comes as a single word, submit, and Ibrahim's answer matches it in kind: I have submitted, to the Lord of the worlds. The exchange gives the root meaning of islam as a personal act before it is the name of a community.

notes.t: aslim and aslamtu share the root of islam and muslim; the verse ties the name to this one exchange between Ibrahim and his Lord.
The same phrase, Lord of the worlds, closes a statement of the Prophet's own prayer, sacrifice, life and death as given over to Allah.

links.why: the same phrase, Lord of the worlds, used for the Prophet's own life and death given over to Allah

132.sense: Ibrahim passes this submission on as a charge to his sons, and Ya'qub does the same to his. The charge is put as a warning about the moment of death: do not let it come to you except as ones who have submitted.

notes.t: The verse folds two men's charges into one sentence, Ibrahim's and Ya'qub's, both handing down the same word for what they leave their sons.
Yusuf, Ya'qub's son, prays at the end of his own account to die as one submitting, using the same word for his death.

links.why: Yusuf's own prayer to die submitting, echoing the charge his father and grandfather passed down

133.sense: The question turns to the hearers directly: were you there when death came to Ya'qub. It then reports his deathbed question to his sons, what they will worship after him, and their answer, naming Allah alone, the one their fathers Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq worshipped, and stating their own submission to Him.

notes.t: The sons answer with a line of three names, not one father alone, tying their worship to the whole lineage rather than to Ya'qub by himself.
Ishaq and Ya'qub are named together as a gift to Ibrahim, each made a prophet, setting out the same three generations elsewhere in the Qur'an.

links.why: Ishaq and Ya'qub named as Ibrahim's gift, the same three generations set out together

134.sense: The verse closes off the appeal to ancestry running through this passage. That nation has already passed on; what it earned belongs to it, what the present hearers earn belongs to them, and no one is questioned about another generation's deeds.

notes.t: kasabat, earned, treats belief and deed as something acquired by a person, not inherited from a lineage: the point being made against resting a claim on Ibrahim's name.
No soul earns except against itself, and no bearer of a burden bears another's: the same principle of individual earning stated directly.

links.why: the same principle stated directly, that no soul earns except against itself

135.sense: The claim is put as a condition: become one or the other and guidance follows. The reply does not accept the terms of the claim; it points instead to Ibrahim, a man of pure faith who lived before the terms of the claim existed, and who was not among those who set up partners with Allah.

notes.t: ḥanīf describes someone inclined away from other gods toward Allah alone, by disposition rather than by formal law; the word recurs for Ibrahim through this section.
A verse in Al Imran states the same denial directly: Ibrahim was not a Jew or a Christian, but a man of pure faith who had submitted, and was not among the polytheists.
Ibrahim is called a man of pure faith, obedient to Allah, chosen and put on a straight path, closing with an instruction to follow his religion.

links.why: the same denial stated directly, that Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian but a man of pure faith who had submitted
the instruction to follow the religion of Ibrahim, a man of pure faith, closing that surah's account of him

136.sense: The instruction is a formula of belief, put in the first person: we believe in Allah, in what was sent to us, and in what was sent to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes, and in what was given to Musa and Isa and to the prophets from their Lord. It closes with a refusal to set the prophets against one another and a statement that submission goes to Allah alone.

notes.t: The verse shifts from unzila, sent down, for Ibrahim's line to ūtiya, given, for Musa and Isa, marking a change in wording rather than a ranking of one revelation above another.
The same statement of belief recurs almost word for word later in the Qur'an, again as something the hearers are told to say.
Allah is described as having ordained for this community the same religion enjoined on Nuh and revealed to Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, with the instruction to keep it and not be divided.

links.why: the same statement of belief, repeated almost word for word later in the Qur'an
the shared religion enjoined on Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, with the same instruction not to divide over it

words.g: then He will suffice you against them

137.sense: The condition runs both ways: if they believe in the same terms the hearers believe in, they are guided; if they turn away, they are simply left in a state of opposition. Allah's sufficiency against them closes the verse, paired with His hearing and knowing.

notes.t: shiqāq comes from shaqq, a split or crack; the root gives the picture of two sides breaking apart from what had been one piece.
A related instruction tells the Prophet, if they argue with you, say I have submitted myself to Allah, and those who follow me, and if they turn away, his duty is only to deliver the message.

links.why: a parallel exchange over the same disagreement, ending the same way: if they turn away, the matter is left with Allah

138.sense: sibghah, color or dye, names the mark Allah gives, set here in place of any human ceremony of joining a community. No one gives a better color than His, and the sentence closes on worship: we are worshippers of Him.

notes.t: sibghah is dye, the kind used to color cloth; the image treats belief as a coloring run through a person rather than a badge worn on the outside.
The word sibghah occurs only here in the Qur'an, but the picture of a disposition set into a person by Allah recurs in the verse on the fiṭrah He shaped people upon.

links.why: the same picture of something set into a person by Allah, there named fiṭrah instead of color

139.sense: The question challenges the ground of the argument itself: Allah is Lord of both sides, not a claim either side owns alone. The verse then separates the two parties by their deeds rather than by their arguments, and closes on sincerity, devotion to Him kept free of other aims.

notes.t: mukhliṣūn comes from khalaṣa, to be clear or purified of mixture; the same root gives ikhlāṣ, sincerity kept free of other aims.
A close parallel: if they deny you, say my deed is for me and your deed is for you, you are free of what I do and I am free of what you do.

links.why: the same separation of deeds, worded almost identically, addressed to a different people who deny the message

140.sense: The question is put directly to whoever makes the claim: do you know better, or does Allah. It then turns to the act of concealment itself, asking who is more unjust than someone holding back a testimony he has from Allah, and closes with a warning that Allah is not unaware of what is done.

notes.t: shahādatan, testimony, treats what these men knew and said as evidence on record, something that can be truthfully reported or hidden, not just a private opinion.
A nearby verse asks the People of the Book directly why they mix truth with falsehood and hide the truth while they know it, the same charge of concealment stated plainly.

links.why: the same charge of knowingly hiding the truth, addressed directly to the People of the Book

141.sense: The formula that closed the appeal to ancestry in verse 134 returns here, word for word, to close the argument over claiming Ibrahim for a single community. That generation has passed on; what it earned is its own, and the present hearers answer for what they earn, not for a claim on someone else's name.

notes.t: The repetition is exact, verse for verse, framing the whole passage between the two occurrences as an argument over inherited claims answered twice with the same statement about individual earning.
The identical verse closes the earlier discussion of Bani Israil's ancestry in this same passage.

links.why: the identical verse, closing the earlier round of this same argument over ancestry
